ἄρα ἐν σώμασιν ἢ χρήμασιν, οὐδὲ κατὰ φύσιν τις σώζεται· κατὰ τοὺς τὰς φύσεις
εἰσάγοντας. Ἐνταῦθα τὴν ψυχὴν ἄντικρυς προεῖπεν σῶμα· καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς δὲ ἐν τοῖς
Εὐαγγελίοις, σῶμα τὴν ψυχὴν ὀνομάζει· Ὁ λύχνος, λέγων, τοῦ σώματός ἐστιν ὁ
ὀφθαλμός· λύχνον μὲν εἶπε τὸν νοῦν· αὐτὸς γάρ ἐστι γνώσεως δεκτικός· σῶμα δὲ τὸ
θυμικὸν καὶ ἐπι 17.192 θυμητικὸν μέρος τῆς ψυχῆς· ὅπερ τινὲς μὲν, ἄλογον· τινὲς δὲ,
παθητικὸν μέρος καλοῦσιν. Ὁ δὲ ἐξ ὧν ἐποίει καὶ διδάσκει ἀγαθῶν, ἐντεῦθεν μὲν
γνῶσιν σω μάτων καὶ ἀσωμάτων ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι δὲ βασιλείαν οὐρανῶν,
περιποιεῖται ἑαυτῷ καὶ τοῖς μαθητιῶσιν· ἐξολλύει δὲ οὐ μόνον τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σῶμα,
ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν, σὺν τοῖς πειθομένοις αὐτῷ, τῷ πυρὶ συναπόλ λυσιν. Οὗτος χειρὶ
χεῖρας ἐμβάλλει ἀδίκως, ὁ κακῶν γινό μενος πραγμάτων καὶ δογμάτων διδάσκαλος·
οὗτος δὲ σπείρει δικαιοσύνην, ὁ περὶ ἀρετῶν καὶ Θεοῦ γνώ σεως προϊέμενος λόγους.

pass_a_gloss: No one is saved by body or wealth, not even by nature—only by those who establish natures. The soul is called body plainly; Christ in the Gospels calls soul body too: the lamp’s body is the eye, he says—he named the lamp the mind, since it receives knowledge; body is the spirited, passionate part of soul, which some name irrational, others emotional. The one who makes and teaches good things gains knowledge of intelligible and immaterial realities now, and later inherits heaven’s kingdom for himself and his learners—not just destroying his own body but also the soul and followers in fire. The one violently grasping hands unjustly teaches evil acts and false beliefs; the one sowing righteousness speaks of virtues and divine knowledge. Those who sow for private gain and increase are opposed by those who gather and reduce—because self-sowers sow spirit and reap life, while gatherers sow flesh and gather corruption. The divine word is grain: Jews concealed it, left it for nations. —As our Savior said in Gospels: no one lights a lamp and puts it under a bowl, but on a stand, to light all in the house. Grain feeds the body; divine knowledge feeds the soul. Whoever holds both kinds of food but gives none, demanding pay from the needy, will be left to the demons. He also writes that he will be cursed by the crowd of angels and all the righteous on judgment day. Living virtue by the Spirit is a skilled work; but the one who does what God owes seeks pleasant partners who accept God’s dues, so they can trade like he does. Those who chase evil, not good, will be set aside. This is the tree of life planted in Eden’s center, which Adam could not touch after sin, having thrown away righteousness’s seeds—from which the tree grows. David says: don’t stay silent toward me, or I’ll be like those going down into the pit. A lawless one who stays silent will be hated by God, not pitied, when he pays rewards to those who accepted his incarnate grace, as the Gospels say: “grace for grace.” Riches of the godless are sin. The righteous will devour them, clearly by good teaching; so in the future age, having become fifteen cities, they’ll get the heavenly inheritance which the impious, having given themselves to impiety, were about to get—but the righteous will take it, as Paul says in 17:193: “But by your hardness and stubborn heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of anger, revelation, and God’s fair judgment.” He will make the good inherit: those who obey him like sons a father will be adopted into heaven’s realm. Like weapons giving safety, they cannot be overcome—no evil resists wisdom, for it is an unbreakable arm; demons cannot stand against it alone. But the foolish find all things, seen and unseen, hostile. He means our bodies are houses—souls dwell in them—owed by those who know reverence and theory; the lawless must learn God’s knowledge and all life-giving commands, so cleansed they see God with mind’s eyes—this blessed goal, kept by all rational nature; the just’s houses stand open to all, as the Lord bids. It follows, then, that no one is preserved in bodily things or in material possessions, nor even according to nature itself. This is because those who introduce or bring about natures—meaning, those who shape or define what things are by their essence—are the ones who determine preservation. At this point, the soul is directly called “body” by the one who speaks plainly. And Christ, too, in the Gospels, refers to the soul as a body—saying, “The lamp,” he declares, “the eye is the body of it.” He called the lamp the mind, for it is inherently receptive of knowledge. But the body, he says, is the spirited and passionate part of the soul—what some call the irrational part, and others, the emotional or suffering part of the soul. Now, the one who, from the things he makes and teaches, produces good outcomes—first, he gains knowledge of both intelligible and immaterial things in the life to come; and in the age to come, he obtains the kingdom of heaven, securing it for himself and for those who learn from him. He does not merely destroy his own body, but also the soul, along with those who follow him, in the fire of shared destruction. This man—this one who wrongly thrusts hand into hand with violence—is the teacher of evil deeds and false doctrines. But this other one—this one who sows righteousness—is the one who advances in speech concerning virtues and the knowledge of God. To those who sow for their own private gain, and who multiply their holdings, stand opposed those who gather and diminish—because those who sow for themselves are, in fact, those who sow into the spirit and reap life; but those who gather and diminish are those who sow into the flesh and thus gather corruption for themselves. The divine word is like grain: which the Jews, having hidden it away, left behind for the Gentiles. —And this is just like what our Savior says in the Gospels: “No one lights a lamp and then puts it under a bushel basket, but on the lampstand, so that it may give light to all in the house.”

Just as grain serves as nourishment for the body, so divine knowledge sustains the soul. Yet the one who possesses the sustenance of both body and soul but refuses to impart it, instead demanding payment from those who lack it, will be abandoned to the demons. Moreover, he writes a curse upon himself, declaring that he will stand under the judgment of the people of the angels and all the righteous on the day of reckoning, and thus he shall be accursed. The practical cultivation of virtues according to the Spirit is a spiritual craft; but the one who performs what is owed to God seeks out delightful companions—those willing to receive what is due to God—so that, just as he himself engages in exchange, they too may engage in mutual giving. As for those who seek not the good but the evil, they shall be left aside. This tree of life is the one planted in the midst of Paradise, whose fruit Adam was forbidden to touch after his sin, having cast away the seeds of righteousness from which the tree of life grows. Lest you remain silent toward me, says David, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit. A lawless person who falls silent will be forsaken by God—that is, hated and not shown mercy—when he renders the rewards due to those who have received the grace of his incarnate economy, as he says in the Gospels: “And grace for grace.” The wealth of the wicked is evil. But the righteous shall consume them, evidently through wholesome teaching; therefore, even in the age to come, having become fifteen cities, they shall inherit the heavenly inheritance which the impious, having surrendered themselves to impiety, were about to receive—but the righteous shall possess it, as Paul also says in 17:193: “But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation and of God’s righteous judgment.”

The good one will act as an heir for those who obey him as sons obey their father, and he will adopt them into the heavenly kingdom. For they are invincible, just as weapons produce safety; for nothing evil can stand against wisdom, because it is an unconquerable weapon; only against this are the demons powerless. But to the foolish, both visible things and incorporeal things are entirely opposed. Here he speaks of the bodies as houses; for houses are the dwellings of souls, and they are owed by those who know piety and possess theoretical knowledge. The lawless must learn not only the knowledge of God, but also every commandment of the life-giving ones, so that, having become pure, they may see God with their intellectual eyes. For this is the blessed end, which every rational nature has preserved. And the houses of the righteous are ready to receive all, as the Lord commands. Now he has spoken of the intentions as the divine visions and the dispositions of the virtues, which he set against the ways of the bold-hearted mind. For from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, as the Lord said; not to do evil, but to do good, the good man intends in his mind. But the bold-hearted, acting and speaking like a fool, will be filled with scourgings, and with the loss of things, and finally will lose his own soul.
